body:
The historical setting

Gautama Buddha lived during a period of important political, economic and intellectual changes in northern India, conventionally placed in the 6th–5th centuries BCE. Larger kingdoms were emerging, towns were expanding, and people were questioning established ideas about religious rituals, suffering and the purpose of life.

This was the age of the Mahajanapadas. Understanding their political organisation helps explain the places Buddha visited, the rulers he encountered and the society in which Buddhism developed.

From Janapadas to Mahajanapadas

The word janapada means the territory where a jana, or a people or clan, settled. Over time, some of these territories developed into larger and more powerful political units called mahajanapadas, meaning great janapadas.

Early Buddhist and Jain texts refer to 16 Mahajanapadas, although their lists are not identical. These states became prominent around the 6th century BCE. Many possessed fortified capitals, organised armies and systems for collecting revenue.

New methods of agriculture helped support this growth. Iron ploughshares made it easier to cultivate certain soils, while improved agricultural production supplied food to expanding towns. Rulers collected taxes to maintain soldiers, officials and fortifications.

The growth of towns also brought merchants, craftspeople, rulers and wandering teachers into closer contact. This environment helped new religious and philosophical ideas reach wider audiences.

Monarchies and Gana-Sanghas

The Mahajanapadas did not all follow the same form of government. Some were monarchies, while others were organised as ganas or sanghas.

FeatureMonarchyGana-Sangha
Political authorityConcentrated in a kingShared among several ruling members or chiefs
Decision-makingKing and his advisersAssemblies of ruling members
ExamplesMagadha and KosalaVajji and Malla
Important distinctionOne principal rulerSeveral members participated in governing

In a gana-sangha, important matters could be discussed in assemblies. However, participation was generally restricted to particular ruling groups. These arrangements were not equivalent to modern democracies based on universal adult voting rights.

The Sakya clan and the Buddha

Siddhartha Gautama belonged to the Sakya clan, a Kshatriya group organised as a small gana. The Sakyas were associated with Kapilavastu, near the present India–Nepal border.

The Sakya territory was much smaller than the major kingdoms of the period and is not included among the standard lists of 16 Mahajanapadas. Buddhist traditions place it within the wider political influence of Kosala.

This explains an important distinction: Buddha belonged to a clan-based political community, but he taught in territories ruled by powerful monarchs as well as in other gana-sanghas.

Prelims focus

  • The 16 Mahajanapadas became prominent around the 6th century BCE.
  • Janapada means the territory in which a people or clan settled.
  • Magadha and Kosala were important monarchies.
  • Vajji and Malla were associated with gana-sangha forms of government.
  • The Buddha belonged to the Sakya clan, associated with Kapilavastu.
  • Trap: The Sakya gana was not one of the standard 16 Mahajanapadas, and ancient gana-sanghas were not modern universal democracies.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 6, Kingdoms, Kings and an Early Republic, printed pp. 56–62; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, ch. 2, Kings, Farmers and Towns, printed pp. 29–31; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, ch. 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, printed pp. 84–86.]

pictures.caption: A growing settlement in northern India during the age of the Mahajanapadas.

title: North India in the Age of the Buddha: Mahajanapadas and Ganas

body:
Birth and early life

Gautama Buddha was known before his enlightenment as Siddhartha Gautama. He was born at Lumbini, which is located in present-day Nepal, and belonged to the Sakya clan associated with Kapilavastu.

Buddhist traditions identify his father as Suddhodana, a chief of the Sakyas, and his mother as Maya, also called Mahamaya. After his mother's death, Siddhartha was cared for by Mahapajapati Gotami, who later became an important member of the Buddhist monastic community.

Later Buddhist biographies identify Siddhartha's wife as Yasodhara and his son as Rahula. These family relationships belong to the traditional account of his life.

Dates and traditional ages

Buddha is conventionally associated with the 6th–5th centuries BCE, but the exact years of his birth and death remain uncertain. Different Buddhist chronological traditions and modern historical estimates do not agree.

In the familiar traditional biography, Siddhartha renounced household life at about 29, attained enlightenment at about 35 and died at about 80. These are useful traditional associations, not independently established dates.

Historical qualification: Lumbini's association with the Buddha's birth is well established in Buddhist tradition and recognised at the historic site. However, precise birth and death years should not be treated as universally settled historical facts.

The 4 sights and the search for an answer

According to the traditional account, Siddhartha grew up in comfortable surroundings but became troubled by the unavoidable realities of human existence.

The famous account of the 4 sights describes encounters with:

  1. An old person: revealing that ageing is unavoidable.
  2. A sick person: revealing human vulnerability to illness.
  3. A dead person: revealing the inevitability of death.
  4. A wandering ascetic: suggesting that a person could leave ordinary household attachments to seek freedom from suffering.

The first 3 sights exposed suffering and impermanence. The fourth suggested a possible way to investigate these problems. They are associated with Siddhartha's decision to seek a deeper understanding of life.

The Great Renunciation

Siddhartha's departure from household life is traditionally called the Great Renunciation or Mahabhinishkramana. He gave up the security of his previous life and became a wandering seeker.

He is traditionally said to have studied under teachers including Alara Kalama and Uddaka Ramaputta. Their meditative disciplines did not, in his understanding, provide the final answer to the problem of suffering.

He also practised severe austerities, including extreme bodily deprivation. Eventually, he rejected the belief that weakening or tormenting the body was itself the way to liberation.

This experience prepared the central distinction of his later teaching: genuine spiritual discipline does not require either unrestricted indulgence in pleasure or destructive self-mortification.

What the life events explain

Siddhartha's early experiences were not merely a series of incidents. They help explain the questions that shaped Buddhism: Why are ageing, sickness, loss and death distressing? Why do people remain dissatisfied even when they obtain what they desire? Can suffering be understood and brought to an end?

The search begun through renunciation led to his later explanation of suffering, craving and the Middle Way.

Prelims focus

  • Birthplace: Lumbini, present-day Nepal.
  • Clan and early home: Sakya and Kapilavastu.
  • Father: Suddhodana; mother: Maya; foster mother: Mahapajapati Gotami.
  • The 4 sights were old age, illness, death and a wandering ascetic.
  • The Great Renunciation was Siddhartha's departure from household life.
  • Trap: The traditional ages 29, 35 and 80 should not be presented as historically certain.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 7, New Questions and Ideas, printed pp. 65–66; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, ch. 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, printed pp. 89–90; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Lumbini, the Birthplace of the Lord Buddha, site description, consulted 18 November 2026; Government of India, Ministry of Tourism, In the Footsteps of the Buddha, 14 September 2020; The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Life of the Buddha, 2003; The Open University, The Dates of the Buddha, 11 February 2020.]

pictures.alt: Siddhartha's early life and 4 sights lead to renunciation, followed by teachers, severe austerities and rejection of bodily deprivation.
pictures.caption: The principal stages of Siddhartha's search before enlightenment.

title: Siddhartha Gautama: Birth, Family and the Great Renunciation

body:
Enlightenment at Bodh Gaya

After abandoning extreme austerities, Siddhartha continued his search through meditation. According to Buddhist tradition, he attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, in present-day Bihar, while meditating beneath a peepal tree.

The tree became known as the Bodhi tree. After his awakening, Siddhartha came to be called the Buddha, meaning the Awakened or Enlightened One.

Bodh Gaya belonged to the wider region of Magadha, an important monarchy of the period. Thus, the place of enlightenment should be associated with both modern Bihar and ancient Magadha.

Enlightenment refers to the insight through which Buddha understood the nature of suffering and the way to its cessation. It was not his birth, first sermon or death.

The journey to Sarnath

Following enlightenment, Buddha travelled to Sarnath, near present-day Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh. Sarnath was traditionally known as Isipatana or Rishipatana and was associated with a Deer Park.

Here, he delivered his first sermon to a group of 5 ascetics who had previously known him during his period of severe austerities.

One of these ascetics, Kondanna, is particularly remembered in Buddhist tradition as an early disciple who understood the teaching.

Dhammacakkappavattana: setting the wheel of teaching in motion

The first sermon is traditionally known in Pali as the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, commonly described as the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma. The Sanskrit-based expression is Dharmachakra Pravartana.

In this teaching, Buddha rejected 2 extremes:

  • Devotion to sensual pleasure and self-indulgence.
  • Severe self-mortification, which causes bodily suffering without producing liberation.

He taught a Middle Way between these extremes. This way is expressed through the Noble Eightfold Path.

The sermon also presented the 4 Noble Truths: the reality of suffering, its origin in craving, the possibility of its cessation, and the path leading to that cessation.

Why the first sermon matters

Enlightenment and teaching were related but distinct events. At Bodh Gaya, Siddhartha attained awakening. At Sarnath, he communicated the path he had discovered to others.

The acceptance of his teaching by the first ascetics is associated with the beginning of the Buddhist Sangha, the community of Buddhist renunciants.

Bodh Gaya is associated with attainment of enlightenment. Sarnath is associated with the first sermon. Both events occurred after the Great Renunciation.

Prelims focus

  • Enlightenment: Bodh Gaya, Bihar, in the ancient region of Magadha.
  • Tree of enlightenment: peepal or Bodhi tree.
  • First sermon: Sarnath, near Varanasi, Uttar Pradesh.
  • The first sermon was delivered to 5 ascetics in the Deer Park.
  • Dhammacakkappavattana refers to the turning of the wheel of Dhamma.
  • Trap: Enlightenment took place at Bodh Gaya, not Sarnath.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 7, New Questions and Ideas, printed pp. 65–66; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, ch. 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, printed pp. 89–92; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Mahabodhi Temple Complex at Bodh Gaya, site description, consulted 18 November 2026; SuttaCentral, Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, translated by Bhikkhu Bodhi, consulted 18 November 2026; Government of India, Ministry of Culture, account of Sarnath and the first sermon, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A seated teacher addresses five ascetics beneath a spreading tree in a peaceful woodland clearing, with two deer nearby.
pictures.caption: The first teaching in the Deer Park at Sarnath, as remembered in Buddhist tradition.

pictures.alt: Buddha attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya in Bihar, ancient Magadha, before teaching 5 ascetics at Sarnath near Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh.
pictures.caption: Enlightenment and the first sermon were different events at different places.

title: Enlightenment at Bodh Gaya and the First Sermon at Sarnath

body:
The central problem addressed by Buddhism

The 4 Noble Truths form the central explanation of suffering and liberation in early Buddhist teaching. They identify a problem, explain its cause, establish that it can cease, and describe the path leading to its cessation.

The Pali word dukkha is often translated as suffering. However, its meaning is wider than physical pain or sadness. It also includes the dissatisfaction and insecurity that arise because pleasant experiences, possessions, relationships and conditions do not remain unchanged.

The 4 Noble Truths explained

  1. The Truth of Suffering (Dukkha): Human existence involves ageing, illness, death, separation from what is loved, contact with what is disliked and failure to obtain what is desired. Even pleasurable experiences cannot provide permanent satisfaction because they change and end.
  2. The Truth of the Origin of Suffering (Samudaya): Suffering arises through craving, called tanha in Pali. Craving includes attachment to sensual pleasures, the wish to maintain a particular form of existence, and the wish for non-existence. It produces continued attachment and dissatisfaction.
  3. The Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (Nirodha): When craving is brought to an end, the suffering sustained by craving can cease. This cessation is associated with nibbana in Pali, or nirvana in Sanskrit.
  4. The Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (Magga): The practical way to end suffering is the Noble Eightfold Path, which develops wisdom, ethical conduct and mental discipline.

Why craving causes dissatisfaction

Suppose a person obtains a possession that has been desired for a long time. The possession may bring happiness, but the person can then become anxious about losing it, dissatisfied with its limitations or eager to obtain something better.

This example illustrates tanha: craving treats changing circumstances as if they could provide lasting security or satisfaction.

The teaching does not mean that every practical intention is harmful. The wish to learn, act responsibly or relieve another person's suffering is not identical to selfish attachment. The distinction concerns the nature of the desire and the attachment associated with it.

Nibbana is not simply physical death

Nibbana means the extinguishing of craving and the ending of the suffering sustained by it. In Buddhist teaching, liberation can be realised during a person's lifetime.

It should therefore not be confused with ordinary physical death. The term parinibbana is used in connection with the final passing of a fully liberated person, including Buddha's death.

The Noble Truths form one connected explanation

The truths should be understood together. The first identifies suffering; the second identifies craving as its origin; the third states that the origin can cease; and the fourth identifies the discipline required to realise that cessation.

The first 2 truths explain the problem. The final 2 describe liberation from it.

Prelims focus

  • First Noble Truth: dukkha, or suffering and unsatisfactoriness.
  • Second Noble Truth: samudaya, the origin of suffering in craving or tanha.
  • Third Noble Truth: nirodha, the cessation of suffering.
  • Fourth Noble Truth: magga, the Noble Eightfold Path.
  • Nibbana is associated with the cessation of craving.
  • Trap: The Fourth Noble Truth identifies the path; it is not the claim that suffering is unavoidable and cannot end.

[Sources: SuttaCentral, Samyutta Nikaya 56.11, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, translated by Bhikkhu Bodhi, section on the 4 Noble Truths, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, ch. 7, New Questions and Ideas, printed pp. 65–66; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, ch. 4, Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings, printed pp. 91–92.]

pictures.caption: The relationship between suffering, craving, cessation and the path.

title: The Four Noble Truths: Suffering, Its Cause and Its Cessation
